You see It means core, identity only lumnik Open llm and rag as well lumnik Pro search_pg or search_opensearch a build with a Search provider INACTIVE, disabled:lumnik.ai.enabled Pro with the AI switched off: installed, not absent. Switching the AI off

Which edition you run decides the rows marked edition below. Editions

docs.title: What an auditor asks
docs.text: Question Answer, in short Page What stops tenant A reading tenant B? PostgreSQL Row-Level Security on every tenanted table; the request role cannot bypass it. RLS Can we plug in our own IdP? Any OIDC issuer. Tested with Keycloak only. Edition: first login needs JIT provisioning, absent from lumnik Open. BYO IdP Is password guessing throttled? The shipped realm has brute-force detection on. With your own IdP it is your IdP's policy. Users & scopes Does a departure cut access, and how fast? Archive the hub row: the next request is refused. Disable in the IdP alone: a live token keeps working until it expires (1 hour on the bundled realm). Offboarding Are stored credentials encrypted? pgcrypto AES-256 under two keys held in .env. No key rotation tooling. Secrets at rest Is our ingested data encrypted at rest? No. Mirror tables and the RAG corpus are plaintext columns. Disk and backup encryption are your layer. Data at rest Is traffic encrypted end to end? TLS at the edge only. Plain HTTP behind it, on your internal network. Data in transit Can we honour access and erasure requests? Access is manual. Erasure of ingested data is a rebuild: delete the entity (for every tenant) and the connector, re-apply, re-ingest. GDPR Who did what, when? Configuration applies and deletes, entity reads, direct searches and data leaving the hub; not questions, SQL, SCIM or webhook settings. The audit trail Can one tenant exhaust our capacity? Chat, RAG search, view generation and direct search are capped per tenant per minute. Single node only. Rate limits Can we recover from data loss? Scripted hot PostgreSQL dump at the cron interval you choose. No point-in-time recovery. Backup & restore How long are ingested rows kept? Until the connector is deleted. GDPR Does the hub log personal data? At the default level the login path logs no subject or issuer, and chat logs counts, never a question or a row. DEBUG may echo data. There is no written log-content policy. Reading the logs Can the model write, or read another tenant? No. Generated SQL runs as lumnik_readonly under RLS: one SELECT, LIMIT 500. No conversation history is stored. Nothing leaves your network unless you configure a cloud provider. Ask honesty How do we report a vulnerability? Email contact@lumnik.fr, subject [lumnik security], never a public issue. Acknowledgment within 72 hours, fix or mitigation within 14 days. Supported: the latest v1.x. SECURITY.md, at the root of every edition

docs.title: The audit trail
docs.text:
Rows land in core.audit_event, each with the acting user and the tenant, within about two seconds of the gesture. A gesture lands once, also when several hub replicas run: the replica that copies it into the trail holds it until that copy is committed, and the others pass over it.

entity_type operation changes carries Written by User CREATE, UPDATE login, email, locked, defaultScope, after the write the users API, lm scope set, JIT first login (with no actor); not SCIM Secret CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE name, description, rotatedAt; never the value lm secret set, lm secret rm Connector APPLY, DELETE name, type, tags, via; manifest_sha256 when via = manifest. Never the configuration see via below Entity APPLY, DELETE scopes; manifest_sha256 on APPLY lm entity apply, lm entity delete Entity READ nothing lm entity get, the entity API Entity EGRESS rows, bytes, SHA-256 of the file lm entity export SearchIndex APPLY, DELETE, REBUILD, CANCEL DELETE by an entity delete names that entity and lands in the tenant that owned the index; REBUILD/CANCEL carry the run id lm search …, lm entity delete Search READ entities hit, hit count; never the query text lm search query, the PWA's Search tab SavedView APPLY, DELETE scope; manifest_sha256 on APPLY lm view apply, lm view rm WorkflowManifest APPLY, UPDATE, DELETE scope; table, column and manifest_sha256 on APPLY; enabled on UPDATE lm workflow apply, disable, enable, rm Process APPLY, UPDATE, DELETE scope; table and manifest_sha256 on APPLY; enabled on UPDATE lm process apply, disable, enable, rm AppRegistration APPLY, DELETE scope, manifest_sha256, demoted_default (the app that lost the default flag) lm app apply, lm app rm Export APPLY scope, entity, manifest_sha256 lm export apply Export EGRESS entity, rows, bytes, SHA-256 of the file, destination kind and location each delivered export run

The via of a Connector row names the gesture:

via Gesture manifest lm apply api lm connector apply, lm connector delete, the TUI's edit scope lm connector scope set csv-ingest lm csv ingest (row carries via, table, tags, refreshed) jdbc-add lm source jdbc add

A write the hub refused leaves no row. A Connector DELETE also drops the connector's tables and run history. App rows land in the tenant of the integrator who wrote them.

A connector and an entity applied, the entity read, then both deleted:

$ lm apply -f erp-customers.yaml
Applied connector "erp-customers" — 1 endpoint
$ lm entity apply -f customer.yaml
Applied entity "Customer" → connector."v_customer"
$ lm entity get Customer --filter email=jeanne.martin@example.com
CUSTOMER_ID  NAME           EMAIL                      CITY  _CONFLICTS
C-1001       Jeanne Martin  jeanne.martin@example.com  Lyon  {}
$ lm entity delete customer
Type 'delete' to delete entity customer — its view, for every tenant: delete
deleted: customer
$ lm connector delete erp-customers
Type 'delete' to delete connector erp-customers (csv-file) — 3 rows of connector.t_erp_customers, its run history and RAG chunks: delete
deleted: erp-customers

lumnik=# SELECT entity_type, operation, changes FROM core.audit_event
         WHERE changes->>'name' = 'erp-customers' OR entity_key = 'Customer' ORDER BY id;
 entity_type | operation |                                                                                  changes
-------------+-----------+----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Connector   | APPLY     | {"via": "manifest", "name": "erp-customers", "tags": ["sales"], "type": "csv-file", "manifest_sha256": "0c34eee4a4c25cb505267a808b61c1ae9402bc1609fb3926eeb1c9ee9f59c9a6"}
 Entity      | APPLY     | {"scopes": ["sales"], "manifest_sha256": "38817cb644e0b38066f8cf07f869397bbeedb01430844b891340b5cb2a44a467"}
 Entity      | READ      | {}
 Entity      | DELETE    | {"scopes": ["sales"]}
 Connector   | DELETE    | {"via": "api", "name": "erp-customers", "tags": ["sales"], "type": "csv-file"}
(5 rows)

To prove which file was applied, compare manifest_sha256 with the file's digest. It matches a UTF-8 file sent as it is, which is what lm apply does:

$ shasum -a 256 erp-customers.yaml
0c34eee4a4c25cb505267a808b61c1ae9402bc1609fb3926eeb1c9ee9f59c9a6  erp-customers.yaml

docs.title: Not recorded
docs.text:
• Anything not in the table above, e.g. webhook targets, notification rules, SCIM tokens, tenants, orgs, hook toggles.
  • Questions asked, the SQL that ran, chat and RAG searches.
  • Connector runs (they have their own run ledger), a connector's endpoint edits, pause and resume.
  • SCIM-driven user writes, deprovisioning included.
  • Archiving a user: it is an ordinary User / UPDATE, indistinguishable from any other edit.

docs.title: Retention and integrity
docs.text:
• A nightly purge deletes rows older than LUMNIK_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 365; 0 keeps forever). There is no per-row erasure.
  • No read surface: query the table directly, as above, as lumnik_admin or as lumnik_app inside the tenant.
  • Append-only for lumnik_app: UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE are revoked. Only lumnik_admin, which runs the purge, can delete.

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
Refusals are logged, not audited. Each leaves one WARN line, never a token; point your SIEM at them. Reading the logs

Gate Log line role Access denied: required=[…], actual=[…], method=… scope Access denied: scope not granted, granted=[…] SCIM SCIM auth refused: GET /scim/v2/… reason=missing or reason=unknown-or-revoked token JWT auth rejected: <reason> deactivated user login denied: user is deactivated or login denied: external identity is deactivated

docs.title: Not built yet
docs.text:
Collect these for your risk register.

Keys & data at rest

  • No master-key rotation. Changing LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY or LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY makes every secret it protects undecryptable; losing it makes them unrecoverable.
  • The backup script does not cover .env: back both keys up separately.
  • The keys sit in .env on the host, in clear. A copy of .env plus a database dump decrypts every stored secret.
  • Ingested data, the RAG corpus and backups are plaintext.

Personal data

  • No DSAR export endpoint. No automated hard-delete of user accounts. No deletion propagation from sources to mirror tables. No API to erase a dead-letter payload. GDPR

Database trust boundary

  • Whoever holds lumnik_admin or the superuser reads every tenant. Code on the admin datasource filters by tenant itself; RLS will not catch a bug there.
  • RLS trusts the tenant the hub resolved from the JWT.
  • Saved views and entity manifests are hub-wide definitions, bound by scope grants. The data they render still goes through RLS.
  • The business-scope boundary inside a tenant is a guard on generated SQL, not a database policy.

Capacity & recovery

  • Rate limiting is in-memory: N replicas means up to N× the configured limit. SCIM is not rate-limited; its bearer is 256 bits of randomness.
  • A dump at your cron interval, no point-in-time recovery: the RPO is that interval.
  • Changing the hub's public origin re-keys every JIT identity: pick it once, early. Keep the same public address

Identity

  • lm_integrator gates the whole platform API but is absent from the roles catalog (GET /api/platform/roles lists lm_superadmin, lm_admin, lm_user). An RBAC inventory taken from that catalog misses it. Roles & permissions
  • The permission catalog is declarative: endpoints are gated by role name.
  • SCIM writes skip the audit trail.
  • Disabling an account in the IdP does not revoke a live access token: archive the hub row. Offboarding

Edition boundary

  • lumnik Open: no JIT provisioning, no SCIM. A token without a user_id claim is refused: 401 {"error":"no external identity resolution in this edition (user_id claim required)"}.
  • lumnik Open: the view-generate and search rate-limit buckets exist; the three chat and RAG search buckets do not, nor do their endpoints.

Supply chain

  • The hub image is published without a signature or an SBOM attestation.

The model

  • No filter sits between ingested text and the model: a source row carrying instructions can steer an answer. It cannot widen the SQL's rights: the query still runs as lumnik_readonly, under RLS, behind the guards.
  • The hub keeps no conversation history; a cloud provider, if you configure one, keeps its own.

docs.text:

docs.title: Bring your own IdP
docs.text:
The hub validates any OIDC issuer generically; there is no Keycloak-specific code. Your IdP authenticates, lumnik creates the user at first login into a tenant you seeded.

Edition

JIT provisioning ships in lumnik Pro only. On lumnik Open every token needs a user_id claim naming a hub row, which a customer IdP does not know. Editions

sequenceDiagram
  participant U as user
  participant I as your IdP
  participant H as hub
  U->>I: login (lm device flow · PWA PKCE)
  I-->>U: access token — aud · tenant_id · groups · sub
  U->>H: request + Bearer
  H->>H: issuer JWKS · aud = lumnik-backend · tenant_id is an integer
  alt first login, no user_id claim
    H->>H: create user (iss, sub) in the token's tenant — the tenant row must exist
  else later login
    H->>H: resolve the same row · deactivated → 403
  end
  H-->>U: 200, under RLS for that tenant

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
• Validation: discovery and JWKS at your issuer URL, aud pinned to lumnik-backend.
  • Tenant: the mandatory tenant_id claim scopes every query through RLS.
  • Identity key: tenant + issuer + subject, created at first login. The same subject in two tenants is two users. No password lives in lumnik; no user list is synced up front.
  • JIT creates users, never tenants. A token naming a tenant with no row fails the first login.
  • Departures ride SCIM. JIT never reactivates a deactivated identity.

docs.title: Before the first login
docs.text:
1. Create the tenant row: POST /api/tenants as lm_superadmin (the gesture); it returns the new id, from 1000 up. Ids 1 (default) and 11 (hubadmin) are seeded at install and taken. Check what exists: 
    lumnik=# SELECT id, code, name FROM identity.tenant ORDER BY id;
 id |   code   |       name
----+----------+------------------
  1 | default  | Default Tenant
 11 | hubadmin | Hub Admin Tenant
  2. Register a client per surface: one for lm (device flow) and, if you use the PWA, the SPA client (public + PKCE). Mind the audience mapper.
  3. Map the claims onto the access token:
Claim Required Carries aud yes exactly lumnik-backend; without it the token never gets past the OIDC layer (401) tenant_id yes the seeded tenant id, as an integer groups yes the role array: lm_user, lm_integrator, lm_admin, plus scope:<tag> grants. Literal lumnik names, flat. Roles user_id no lumnik's internal user id, only if your IdP knows it (the bundled realm does). Absent: JIT resolves the user by issuer + subject. Present but naming no row: see troubleshooting name, email no profile fields, used at first-login creation only
  • The subject side of the key is sub by default; OIDC_SUBJECT_CLAIM names another claim (see Entra below). The shipped compose file and Helm chart do not pass this variable to the hub.
  • Malformed claims are rejected, never repaired: a non-integer tenant_id, an oversized issuer or subject each fail with their own 401 (troubleshooting). A bad profile claim never blocks a login: a long name is clamped, an invalid email dropped.
  • The bundled accounts occupy (tenant 1, integrator) and (tenant 11, hubadmin) on every hub. An IdP whose subject is a username must not reuse those logins in those tenants.

docs.title: What JIT creates, and what it refuses
docs.text:
• Creates, on first login without user_id: one user in the token's tenant. Login = subject, display name from name (fallback: subject), optional email.
  • Resolves the same row on every later login.
  • Refuses a deactivated identity with 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"}. Only an admin, or a SCIM re-activation you control, brings a user back.

docs.title: Keycloak walkthrough
docs.text:
The shipped realm is the working reference; copy its mapper shapes onto your client:

Step Configuration 1. Realm roles create lm_user, lm_integrator, lm_admin, and scope:<tag> roles if you restrict users by scope. Assign them to users or groups; the hub matches names flat 2. tenant_id mapper User Attribute mapper: attribute tenant_id, claim tenant_id, JSON type long, on the access token 3. groups mapper User Realm Role mapper: claim name groups, multivalued, on the access token 4. Audience mapper Audience mapper adding lumnik-backend to the access token, on every client that calls the hub 5. lm client OIDC client with device flow; point the CLI at it: lm config set-context … --oidc-issuer https://idp.example.com/realms/corp --oidc-client-id <client>

docs.title: Okta / Entra ID notes
docs.text:
• One layer moves to your IdP: the bundled realm throttles password guessing (brute-force detection on). With your own IdP, lockout is your IdP's policy; lumnik never sees a password attempt.
  • Tested with Keycloak only. Okta and Entra need only discovery, JWKS and the claims above; neither has been run against a live hub.
  • Okta: custom claims and a custom audience need a custom authorization server. Map groups to the lumnik role names, not Okta group ids.
  • Entra ID: sub is pairwise per app registration; re-registering the app mints new subjects and orphans every JIT identity. Prefer OIDC_SUBJECT_CLAIM=oid. Entra's default groups claim emits GUIDs: use a claims-mapping policy or app roles to carry the literal lm_* names.
  • SAML-only IdPs (ADFS and friends): not supported by direct trust. Front them with a broker (a Keycloak you or the customer operates) and point lumnik at the broker.

docs.title: Kubernetes: auth.mode=oidc-external
docs.text:
Cloud edition. Trust the customer's issuer, deploy no Keycloak. Set the mode explicitly: the chart's default, oidc, deploys its own Keycloak instead.

# deploy/helm/lumnik/values.yaml
auth:
  mode: oidc-external

oidc:
  external:
    issuerUrl: "https://idp.customer.com/realms/corp"   # discovery/JWKS
    tokenIssuer: ""   # token `iss` to validate; defaults to issuerUrl.
                      # Set ONLY when it differs (a port-forward split on kind).
  • The chart fails fast: a typo'd auth.mode aborts helm install; oidc-external with an empty issuerUrl refuses to render.
  • Both oidc and oidc-external run the hub in production mode (dev-bypass off).
  • Rehearse it locally, with a stand-in "customer IdP" in its own namespace and no Keycloak in the release:
make k8s-up-oidc-external

A real customer IdP is then an issuerUrl swap. Leave tokenIssuer empty in real deployments.

docs.title: The PWA client (lumnik-spa)
docs.text:
The audience mapper

The hub pins aud: lumnik-backend, and a freshly created SPA client emits no audience by default. Symptom: every PWA call is a 401 while lm works fine. Register the SPA client as public + PKCE (S256), redirect URI https://<hub-origin>/app/*, and the audience mapper on the access token. The PWA

docs.title: Keep the same public address
docs.text:
Pick the hub's public address once, before the first real login.

  • lumnik knows a user by the issuer URL + the subject in the token.
  • Change the scheme (http → https), the hostname or the issuer path, and the issuer changes. The same person then logs in as a new user, detached from their history.
  • This bites on a move to TLS, a new hostname, or a restore onto another address.

Moved anyway? Point the old users at the new issuer, once, before they log in again:

docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml exec postgres psql -U lumnik -d lumnik -c \
  "UPDATE identity.app_user SET idp_issuer = 'https://new.example/realms/lumnik'
   WHERE idp_issuer = 'http://localhost:8180/realms/lumnik'"

Users who already logged in under the new issuer have a second row: archive it first, or accept that they start fresh.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix 401 {"error":"missing or invalid tenant_id claim"} No tenant_id on the access token, or a non-integer value Add or fix the tenant_id mapper (JSON type long, access token) 401 with no lumnik error body Rejected by the OIDC layer: wrong or missing aud, or iss ≠ the configured issuer Add the audience mapper; check issuerUrl/tokenIssuer match the token's iss 401 {"error":"missing subject/issuer claim"} No user_id claim and no subject claim Check OIDC_SUBJECT_CLAIM names a claim the IdP emits 401 {"error":"no external identity resolution in this edition (user_id claim required)"} No user_id claim on a lumnik Open build Run lumnik Pro, or emit user_id 401 {"error":"subject/issuer claim too long"} iss or subject exceeds 255 characters; never truncated, that would change the identity Use a shorter stable claim (Entra oid) 404 {"error":"no user record on this hub for user_id N"} on lm scope The IdP emits a user_id that names no hub row Point it at an existing row, or drop it so JIT resolves the user (Pro) First login 500, logs show fk_user_tenant Tenant row not seeded Seed the tenant, retry 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"} Identity exists but was deactivated (a SCIM departure) Reactivate via admin or SCIM; JIT never resurrects 403 on every endpoint despite a valid login groups missing, or carrying IdP-native names Map roles into groups as literal lm_* names Login error after moving to TLS or a new hostname The issuer changed Keep the same public address

docs.title: Credentials a source writes back
docs.text: Some APIs repeat the credential they received: a 401 that quotes the Authorization header, a GraphQL error that prints it, a SOAP Fault, a debug page that shows its query string. This page states what lumnik hides from such a response, where, and what it cannot hide.

docs.title: Where it applies
docs.text:
Every request a REST, GraphQL or SOAP connector sends with its credential: the pages of a run, lm source rest test, and lm source rest probe. The response is cleaned once, as it arrives, so everything after it sees the same text: a run's failure message, the sample lm source rest test returns, the retries, and the rows written to the table.

The OAuth2 token request is not cleaned: its answer is the token, and lumnik never quotes it.

docs.title: The rules, and why
docs.text: Rule Why The whole Authorization value is replaced in every response: Bearer eyJh… becomes Bearer <redacted>. A query parameter whose name says it is a credential (apikey=…, token=…) becomes apikey=<redacted>. No row writes Bearer followed by your token, or apikey= followed by your key. These forms are a credential wherever they appear, whatever their length. A response that is not ingested loses the bare value too: an HTTP error, a GraphQL errors answer, a SOAP Fault. The value is replaced as sent, JSON-escaped (\/) and URL-encoded. The user and password of a Basic credential are replaced decoded as well. This text only ever reaches a failure message or a test sample, never your tables, so replacing too much costs nothing. In that same response, a value shorter than 8 characters is replaced only where it stands alone, not inside a longer word or number. A short value is often part of the error text itself. Replacing it inside every word would make the message unreadable. A response that is ingested never loses a bare value. A token 12345678 and a "customer_id": 12345678 are the same text. Rewriting it would change your data, and no length tells one from the other. An OAuth2 access_token shorter than 8 characters is refused before the first page. No other credential is refused for its length. lumnik obtains that token itself, so it can refuse one too short to keep out of an error text. A static key is yours, and lumnik will not lock you out for its length. In an XML or HTML response the marker is written <redacted>. A parser reads it back as <redacted>. <redacted> is a tag in markup. Writing it raw would break the envelope: a SOAP page would fail to parse, and a Fault would no longer be reported as one.

docs.title: What is not covered
docs.text: Case What happens A credential sent in the request body: a {{secret:…}} inside a SOAP envelope, a form or JSON login. Only headers and query parameters are known as credentials. A source that echoes a body credential shows it in the failure message. Prefer a header credential where the API offers one. A header whose name does not contain key, token, secret, password or auth, for example X-Signature or Cookie. It is not treated as a credential, and an echo of it is not hidden. An echo in a response header. Nothing lumnik prints shows a response header in full. A redirect's failure message names its host only.

docs.title: GDPR & personal data
docs.text:
Where personal data can live in a lumnik installation, what erasure does today, and what is not built.

lumnik is self-hosted software, not a service: no data reaches a lumnik cloud. You remain the controller or processor of the data it touches. This page is an engineering map, not legal advice.

docs.title: The posture, in three sentences
docs.text:
• Nothing leaves your infrastructure by default. Chat and embeddings run on a local model runtime (Ollama). Once you configure a cloud LLM provider, questions and grounding chunks are sent to it.
  • lumnik is a read-only mirror. Ingestion never writes back. Ask-to-SQL runs under a read-only database role behind its guards. The hub keeps no conversation history.
  • Isolation is enforced in the database. PostgreSQL Row-Level Security per tenant (RLS); chat, search and entity reads are also bound per business scope.

docs.title: Where personal data can live
docs.text:
Store What lands there Lifecycle identity schema user accounts: login, display name, email archive or soft-delete; the row stays until an operator deletes it connector.t_* mirror tables whatever your sources contain kept until the connector is deleted; see the per-type list below rag.chunk corpus text chunks and embeddings derived from ingested rows a changed row adds a chunk, the old one stays; deleting the connector removes every chunk it produced Dead letters the raw payload of rows a run set aside, for any reason kept with the connector; lm dlq discard marks an entry handled and keeps the payload Event outbox entity name, a key hash, the operation purged nightly past LUMNIK_EVENTS_RETENTION_DAYS (default 30) Audit trail the acting user and what they wrote, read or exported. What it records purged nightly past LUMNIK_AUDIT_RETENTION_DAYS (default 365, 0 = forever). No per-row erasure Webhook payloads the column values a kind: Process template references, posted to the tenant's target URL (n8n, Make, your endpoint); HMAC-signed when a secret is set, otherwise protected only by that URL's TLS leaves lumnik; retention is the receiver's Webhook delivery history the posted payload and the receiver's response body, plus status and attempts purged nightly past LUMNIK_WEBHOOKS_DELIVERY_RETENTION_DAYS (default 90, 0 = forever) Keycloak its own user store: credentials, sessions your realm, your policies Backups whatever you back up yours entirely

How a change at the source reaches the mirror tables:

Connector Changed row Row deleted at the source jdbc-generic replaced by source key stays in the mirror rest-generic (GraphQL, SOAP included) replaced by its unique_key stays in the mirror csv-file reading one local file (no glob) replaced: the old version is removed by the next run that reads the whole file; a run that would remove more than 30 % of the rows is refused removed the same way csv-file reading a folder, a glob, SFTP or S3; kafka added as a new row; the old version stays stays in the mirror

docs.title: The rights, in practice
docs.text:
Access and portability

  • lm entity get gives structured access to one person's rows; read-only SQL covers the rest.

    $ lm entity get Customer --filter email=jeanne.martin@example.com
CUSTOMER_ID  NAME           EMAIL                      CITY  _CONFLICTS
C-1001       Jeanne Martin  jeanne.martin@example.com  Lyon  {}

  • No one-click DSAR export. Assembling an answer is a query your integrator writes.

Rectification

  • Fix the data in the source. On a jdbc-generic, rest-generic or one-file csv-file connector, the mirror follows on the next run. On the others, the old value stays in the mirror next to the new one: erase it as below.
  • The corpus gains a chunk for the corrected row and keeps the chunk carrying the old value until the connector is deleted and re-ingested (below).
  • Ingested rows cannot be edited in lumnik.

Erasure of a person in your data

flowchart LR
  s["1. erase in the<br/>source system"] --> e["2. lm entity delete<br/>(every tenant)"]
  e --> d["lm connector delete"]
  d --> t["mirror tables<br/>purged"]
  d --> c["every RAG chunk<br/>it produced, removed"]
  d --> r["3. re-apply,<br/>re-ingest"]
  1. Erase in the source first; it is the system of record. Save the entity and SearchIndex manifests you will re-apply in step 3: no lm command gives them back once deleted.
  2. Delete every entity that reads the connector's tables (lm connector delete names it), then delete the connector.
  3. Re-apply the connector, the entity and its SearchIndex, then re-ingest.

An entity is shared by every tenant

Deleting it drops its view and every SearchIndex over it in all tenants, until step 3 re-applies them. A SearchIndex belongs to one tenant: each tenant re-applies its own. Views, app screens and Search over that entity are empty in the meantime.

$ lm connector delete erp-customers --dry-run
Error: API error 409: table connector.t_erp_customers feeds entity customer — remove the entity first (lm entity delete customer)
$ lm entity delete customer
Type 'delete' to delete entity customer — its view, for every tenant, and search index customers: delete
deleted: customer
$ lm connector delete erp-customers
Type 'delete' to delete connector erp-customers (csv-file) — 3 rows of connector.t_erp_customers, its run history and RAG chunks: delete
deleted: erp-customers

lumnik=# SELECT count(*) FROM connector.t_erp_customers;
ERROR:  relation "connector.t_erp_customers" does not exist
  • A table another connector also writes keeps that connector's rows.
  • Deleting rows from connector.t_* by hand is not enough: their chunks stay until the connector itself is deleted.

Erasure of a lumnik user account

  • DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id} archives (archived_at); SCIM DELETE soft-deletes (deleted_at). lm has no command for either. Deactivate vs erase
  • Either way the next request is refused with 403, valid token or not, and the account drops out of listings.
  • Neither deletes the row, and neither removes anything from the audit trail. Audit rows go only with the nightly retention purge.

docs.title: Not built yet, recorded not hidden
docs.text:
• No automated hard-delete or pseudonymisation of user accounts. An archived or soft-deleted user stays in the identity schema until an operator deletes the row.
  • No DSAR export endpoint. Access is manual.
  • No deletion propagation from sources to mirror tables. Erasure is the rebuild above.
  • No API to erase a dead-letter payload.
  • The audit trail is narrow: no SCIM writes, nothing outside its table, no read surface, no per-row erasure. Not recorded

docs.title: Tenants, users & scopes
docs.text: Identity lives in Keycloak, not in lumnik. Creating a user, granting a role, and assigning a scope are console gestures; the hub follows the token. lm has no command for users, roles or tenants.

docs.title: How lumnik identifies a user
docs.text:
lumnik trusts four claims from the access token:

Claim Purpose aud identifies the intended API — must contain lumnik-backend tenant_id which tenant the user belongs to groups the realm roles: lm_* open surfaces, scope:* limit data access user_id optional — binds the token to an existing hub row

The bundled realm lumnik already maps the tenant_id and user_id user attributes onto those claims. You set attributes and roles; nothing else.

  • With a user_id: the account is bound to that existing hub row. The bundled integrator (user_id=1) has its row seeded at install.
  • Without a user_id: depends on the edition, see Add a user.

For an external IdP, see Bring your own IdP and SCIM.

docs.title: The console
docs.text:
• http://localhost:8180, realm lumnik, admin credentials from your .env.
  • Brute-force detection is on: temporary lockout at Keycloak's defaults. Tune it under Realm settings → Security defenses.
  • Local only. The compose pins Keycloak to 127.0.0.1, and the TLS proxy proxies login, tokens and the account page, never the admin console. On a remote host, use an SSH tunnel: reach the hub from another machine.

Helm (cloud edition): the bundled Keycloak keeps nothing

With auth.mode=oidc, the chart's Keycloak re-imports its realm at every pod start. Users, roles, attributes and Enabled: off set in the console disappear at the next restart. On Helm, manage users in your own IdP (auth.mode=oidc-external, Bring your own IdP).

docs.title: Add a user
docs.text:
1. Users → Add user: username, email, Create.
  2. Credentials tab: set a password, or let your IdP federation handle it.
  3. Attributes tab: tenant_id = the tenant's numeric id.
  4. Role mapping tab → Assign role → lm_user, plus any scope:* role.

Edition

  • lumnik Pro: nothing else to do. The first login creates the hub row (JIT provisioning).
  • lumnik Open (no JIT): without a user_id attribute the token is refused — 401 {"error":"no external identity resolution in this edition (user_id claim required)"}. Complete the mapping yourself:
    1. Create the hub row: POST /api/tenants/{tid}/users, as an lm_admin of that tenant.
    2. Note the id it returns.
    3. Add it as the account's user_id attribute.

POST /api/tenants/{tid}/users creates a hub row, not a login: nobody can authenticate as it until a Keycloak account points at it.

docs.title: Grant (or revoke) a business scope
docs.text:
Scope roles are created on demand. The shipped realm has none: zero scope:* roles means unscoped, tenant-wide.

  1. Realm roles → Create role: name it scope:ventes, the tag your manifests use in spec.scope.
  2. Users → the user → Role mapping → Assign role → scope:ventes.

To revoke, remove that role from the same Role mapping tab.

From their next token the user is bound:

  • chat, search, views and entity reads answer only inside granted scopes; anything else is 403 {"error":"scope not granted"};
  • the decision inbox lists only decisions in the granted scopes; an id from another scope is a 404;
  • an integrator administers only the connectors whose scopes they hold all of. What they see

Removing the last scope role widens access

A user with no scope:* roles has tenant-wide access. Revoking their last scope role restores access to every scope in the tenant.

flowchart LR
  u0["no scope:* role"] -->|"tenant-wide"| all
  ua["scope:ventes"] --> V
  ua -.->|"403 scope not granted"| S
  subgraph all["one tenant's data"]
    V[("scope: ventes")]
    S[("scope: stock")]
  end

docs.title: Make someone admin, integrator, superadmin
docs.text: Same Role mapping gesture. Roles are separate, not ranked: an integrator is not automatically an admin. What each one opens: Roles & permissions.

docs.title: Onboard a new tenant
docs.text:
1. Create the tenant, as lm_superadmin (the bundled hubadmin account):

curl -s -X POST https://your-hub.example.com/api/tenants \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"code": "ACME", "name": "Acme Corp"}'    # both required; note the returned id

$TOKEN is a hubadmin token: mint it as in Test the API, with username=hubadmin and HUBADMIN_PASSWORD.

2. Create its first administrator: a Keycloak account as in Add a user, with tenant_id = the id returned above and the roles lm_user + lm_admin.

Edition Then lumnik Pro Leave user_id unset. The first login creates the hub row in the new tenant. lumnik Open The account needs a hub row in the new tenant, and POST /api/tenants/{tid}/users answers 403 (empty body) to any token whose tenant_id is not {tid}, hubadmin included.

On lumnik Open, that call passes only for a token holding lm_superadmin and lm_admin plus an acting_as_tenant: <tid> claim (impersonation). The bundled realm maps no such claim.

RLS fences every read and write of the new tenant's users to it from their first request.

docs.title: Offboard someone
docs.text: Archive the hub row, then disable the Keycloak account. The users API's DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id} (as lm_admin) archives; the next request is refused: 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"}. Why both, and how fast each acts: The clock.

docs.text:
• Roles & permissions · Bring your own IdP
  • SCIM · Offboarding · Scopes

docs.title: Offboarding the integrator
docs.text: SCIM covers a business user's departure. This page covers the other one every security officer documents: the integrator whose mission ends. What they could touch, and the last-day checklist.

docs.title: The access footprint
docs.text: They held It opens It lives A realm account with lm_integrator connectors, runs, secrets metadata, views, workflows; usually lm_admin on top (entities, processes, secrets, discovery) — the roles your IdP or the bundled realm The lm CLI session whatever those roles open, from their workstation ~/.lm/config.yaml on their machine The install's .env both master keys, the entity-resolution HMAC secret, the Postgres and Keycloak admin passwords, the bundled accounts' passwords, the three database role passwords the server they installed Database credentials lumnik_admin bypasses RLS anyone who read that .env SCIM tokens, if minted the /scim/v2/* provisioning surface revocable, effect immediate

docs.title: The clock
docs.text:
Two gestures, two clocks. By default the hub checks a token against the IdP's keys only, not whether the account still exists.

Gesture Stops A live access token Archive the hub row: DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id} as lm_admin, or SCIM active: false the very next request, with or without a user_id claim refused at once Disable the account in the IdP (Keycloak Enabled: off) new logins and token refreshes stays valid until it expires: 1 hour on the bundled realm; the refresh chain dies 24 hours after login at the latest, about 30 minutes idle Disable the account in the IdP, with IdP verification on every request: the hub asks the IdP's UserInfo endpoint and fails authentication when it refuses refused on the IdP's answer

Do both. Your own IdP's lifespans may differ.

IdP verification is off by default and costs one IdP round trip per request. On Helm, set auth.verifyWithIdp=true. The self-host compose file does not pass its variable, LUMNIK_AUTH_VERIFY_WITH_IDP, to the hub.

docs.title: The last-day checklist
docs.text:
lm has no command for users or SCIM tokens: steps 1 and 2 are HTTP calls as an lm_admin of the tenant. Check before the last day that the departing consultant is not the only one.

  1. Archive the hub row, then disable the IdP account.
    • Archive: DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/users/{id} (or SCIM active: false). Their next lm call prints Error: access refused (403): user is deactivated.
    • Disable: console at http://localhost:8180, realm lumnik → Users → the account → Enabled: off. No new token is issued. On Helm's bundled Keycloak this does not survive a pod restart: there, archiving the hub row is the step that lasts.
  2. Revoke any SCIM token they minted: DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens/{id}, immediate. Token lifecycle

  3. Change every password they read in .env, as a planned window, not a 5 p.m. gesture. The stack restarts.

    • The bundled accounts — HUBADMIN_PASSWORD (hubadmin, superadmin) and INTEGRATOR_PASSWORD — and the three database role passwords: put new values in .env, then re-run up.sh with the flags you installed with. It sets them all again:

        hubadmin: per-install password set (HUBADMIN_PASSWORD in .env)
  integrator: per-install password set (INTEGRATOR_PASSWORD in .env)

    On a TLS install, run the overlay command again afterwards: up.sh leaves it out. - The Postgres superuser: up.sh does not change it. Set it in the database, then the same value as POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env:

    ```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.selfhost.yml exec postgres \
  psql -U lumnik -d lumnik -c "ALTER ROLE lumnik PASSWORD 'the-new-password'"
```
    • The Keycloak admin password: change it in the console (realm master → Users → admin → Credentials), then the same value as KEYCLOAK_ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env. With only one of the two, the next up.sh prints could not obtain a Keycloak admin token.
    • The master keys cannot be changed in place. The only path is a new key plus re-entering every stored secret by hand. The warning
    • Their workstation. You cannot wipe ~/.lm/config.yaml remotely; step 1 makes its token useless.
    • Host access is your infrastructure's offboarding: SSH keys, VPN, sudo on the server they installed.

docs.title: Known gaps
docs.text:
• No product surface lists "everything user X can reach" or their active sessions.
  • What they left behind stays running: connectors, mappings and .kts hooks, which are code the hub keeps executing.
  • A copy of .env plus any database dump decrypts every stored secret: the master keys cannot be changed in place (step 3).

docs.title: Row-Level Security & database roles
docs.text:
Every tenant's rows are isolated by PostgreSQL itself. The role the hub uses for requests cannot bypass the policy, and the role under LLM-generated SQL cannot write.

Roles lumnik_app (requests) · lumnik_readonly (LLM-generated SQL, views, exports) · lumnik_admin (migrations, DDL, purge) Policy tenant_id = current tenant; no tenant set means zero rows, never an error, never every row Coverage every tenanted table, including the connector.t_* tables ingestion creates Encrypted at rest tenant secrets, connector and webhook credentials only; ingested data is plaintext TLS terminates at the edge you put in front; plain HTTP behind it 
flowchart LR
  req["request path — JWT"] --> app["lumnik_app<br/>RLS enforced"]
  llm["read-only paths —<br/>ask · views · exports ·<br/>search projection"] --> ro["lumnik_readonly<br/>RLS · read-only ·<br/>empty search_path"]
  ops["migrations · dynamic DDL ·<br/>purge · dormancy sweep"] --> adm["lumnik_admin<br/>BYPASSRLS · owns the tables"]
  app -->|"SET LOCAL tenant"| t[("tenant-stamped<br/>tables")]
  ro -->|"SET LOCAL tenant"| t
  adm -->|"deliberate cross-tenant"| t

docs.title: The three database roles
docs.text:
Created at install by the PostgreSQL init script, outside the migrations:

Role Can Cannot Used for lumnik_app read and write rows, under RLS bypass a policy; own a table every request the hub serves lumnik_readonly SELECT, under RLS; the session is read-only write anything; resolve an unqualified table name ask-to-SQL, kind:View render and detail, workflow data checks, the Search projection, export runs, lm entity export lumnik_admin everything; bypasses RLS; owns every table be enlisted in a request transaction by accident migrations, dynamic table DDL, retention purges, connector delete, secret resolution, the workflow dormancy sweep
  • lumnik_app owns nothing. PostgreSQL lets a table's owner bypass its own policies; that rule never applies to a request.
  • See the roles answer a query live: Verify it yourself.

docs.title: How a query gets its tenant
docs.text:
• The hub resolves the tenant from the JWT's tenant_id claim, then issues SET LOCAL app.current_tenant = '<id>' once per transaction. SET LOCAL dies with the transaction; nothing leaks onto the pooled connection.
  • Background work runs as the system sentinel '0'. A token claiming a tenant of 0 or below is not refused: the hub sets no tenant on its connections, so the request runs and sees zero rows. It is never elevated to the sentinel.
  • On the read-only datasource the same tenant is set, the session is read-only, and search_path is empty: every query must name the schema it reads.

docs.title: The policy shape
docs.text:
USING (tenant_id = NULLIF(current_setting('app.current_tenant', true), '')::bigint)
  • No tenant set, or set to '': the predicate is NULL and the query returns zero rows.
  • A handful of hub-wide bookkeeping tables (run ledger, event outbox) also accept the '0' sentinel, so background work can see across tenants on purpose.
  • Tables ingestion creates on the fly (connector.t_* and the mapping targets) get the same policy the moment they are created.
  • Saved views and entity manifests carry no tenant_id: they are hub-wide definitions, bound to users by scope grants. The rows they render still pass through RLS.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
• All three passwords are generated per install and injected as environment variables: LUMNIK_APP_DB_PASSWORD, LUMNIK_ADMIN_DB_PASSWORD, LUMNIK_READONLY_DB_PASSWORD.
  • Self-host rotation: put the new value in .env, re-run deploy/selfhost/up.sh with the flags you installed with. Every run sets the three roles' passwords to the .env values. On a TLS install, run the overlay command again afterwards.
  • Helm: the release Secret carries the three values. On a cluster with an existing volume, rotate at the database (ALTER ROLE … PASSWORD) and upgrade with the matching values.

docs.title: What RLS does NOT protect against
docs.text:
• The admin datasource. lumnik_admin bypasses RLS. Code using it filters by tenant itself; a bug there is a cross-tenant bug RLS will not catch.
  • The database superuser, or anyone holding the lumnik_admin credentials.
  • A wrong tenant upstream. RLS trusts app.current_tenant. The request filter that resolves it from the JWT is part of the trusted computing base.

docs.title: Secrets at rest: the master key
docs.text:
Two keys. No rotation. No recovery.

Back up LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY and LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY somewhere safe, today: both live in .env, which the backup script does not copy. Change one and the secrets it protects become undecryptable. Lose one and they are unrecoverable. A key change means re-entering every secret by hand.

What is encrypted tenant secrets, the lm secret store How pgcrypto pgp_sym_encrypt, AES-256 The key LUMNIK_SECRET_MASTER_KEY, generated at install with openssl rand -base64 32 Refuses to boot on a blank, placeholder, or short (< 16 characters) key Changing one secret's value supported: lm secret set NAME again prints Updated secret "NAME" Changing a key not supported
  • The second key, LUMNIK_CRYPTO_SECRET_KEY, protects connector and webhook credentials the same way.
$ lm secret set SFTP_ERP_PASSWORD
Value for SFTP_ERP_PASSWORD:
Created secret "SFTP_ERP_PASSWORD"
$ lm secret list
NAME                           ROTATED_AT                     DESCRIPTION
ACME_API_KEY                   -
ACME_BASIC_PW                  -
SFTP_ERP_PASSWORD              -

docs.title: Data at rest: what is encrypted, and what is not
docs.text:
• Encrypted: tenant secrets and connector/webhook credentials, under the two keys above.
  • Plaintext: everything you ingest. connector.t_* mirror tables and the rag.chunk corpus are ordinary PostgreSQL columns, readable to anyone who can query the database directly.
  • Disk, volume and backup encryption are the operator's layer, as for any database.

docs.title: Data in transit: where TLS stops
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  b["browser · lm · IdP"] ==>|"HTTPS"| edge["TLS edge<br/>Caddy proxy · your proxy · k8s Gateway"]
  edge -->|"HTTP"| hub["hub :8080"]
  hub -->|"JDBC, no sslmode"| pg[("PostgreSQL")]
  hub -->|"HTTP"| ollama["Ollama"]
  edge -->|"HTTP"| kc["Keycloak :8180"]
  • The hub itself speaks plain HTTP on port 8080. There is no https:// origin in the application.
  • Self-host: the optional TLS proxy terminates HTTPS and proxies to the hub and Keycloak over the compose network. Skip it and the hub answers in the clear on whatever you exposed port 8080 to.
  • Kubernetes: the Gateway terminates TLS from a secret (self-signed by up.sh unless you supply your own); Gateway→pod is plain HTTP inside the cluster.
  • Behind the edge nothing is encrypted: hub↔PostgreSQL, hub↔Ollama, proxy↔hub. Keep the database and model ports on a private network; that is the operator's job.

docs.title: Roles & permissions
docs.text:
Four lm_* realm roles open surfaces; scope:<tag> roles narrow which data those surfaces show. Matching is flat, no hierarchy: every role a user needs is granted explicitly.

flowchart LR
  u["lm_user"] --> s1["business reads —<br/>entities · views · chat"]
  i["lm_integrator"] --> s2["/api/platform/* —<br/>connectors · runs · views · exports"]
  a["lm_admin"] --> s3["entities · processes · secrets ·<br/>outputs · users"]
  sa["lm_superadmin"] --> s4["platform-wide —<br/>tenant list · impersonation"]
  sc["scope:achat · scope:stock …"] -.->|"limits WHICH data,<br/>inside what a role opened"| s1
Role Opens lm_user the app surface: entities, views, chat, inbox, the PWA lm_integrator the platform surface lm drives: connectors, runs, dead letters, views, apps, workflows, search indexes, exports lm_admin entities, processes, secrets (write), the guided JDBC flow, schema discovery, workflow observations, outputs, email rules, users, SCIM tokens lm_superadmin cross-tenant: tenant list, tenant CRUD, impersonation; the only role with wildcard: true scope:<tag> not a surface: a fence. One or more binds the user to those scopes; none means tenant-wide. Scopes
  • No hierarchy. lm_admin does not imply lm_user. The bundled realm grants integrator three roles (integrator, admin, user) for that reason. An integrator needs all three: with lm_integrator alone, lm entity apply already answers 403.
  • Roles live in the IdP. Granting one is a Keycloak gesture: Tenants, users & scopes.
  • Three gates, three refusals. Which one answered tells you what to grant; see Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Which role for which gesture
docs.text:
You run Roles it needs lm connector …, lm run …, lm dlq …, lm endpoint …, lm csv ingest, lm apply -f (connector) lm_integrator lm view apply, lm app apply, lm workflow …, lm search … (but query), lm export …, lm hook scripts, lm secret list lm_integrator lm entity apply, lm entity delete, lm entity resolve, lm entity assert-same, lm entity assert-distinct lm_admin lm process … (every subcommand, list included) lm_admin lm secret set, lm secret rm lm_integrator and lm_admin lm source jdbc …, lm source schema, lm source rediscover, lm rag status, lm hook get lm_integrator and lm_admin lm observations … lm_integrator and lm_admin lm integration …, lm outputs … lm_integrator and lm_admin lm notify …, user and SCIM token administration lm_admin lm entity get, lm view … (read), lm inbox, lm ask, lm chat, lm search query, the PWA lm_user

The bundled integrator account holds the three roles, so every line works with it. Check this table when the client's own IdP grants the roles.

docs.title: A hub with no login: dev-bypass
docs.text:
A hub in dev-bypass checks no token: every caller is lm_superadmin, lm_admin and lm_user, and picks any tenant with the X-Tenant-ID header.

  • The self-host stack (up.sh) never runs in dev-bypass.
  • The Helm chart (cloud edition) defaults to auth.mode: oidc. It renders dev-bypass only with auth.iUnderstandNoAuth=true as well; make k8s-up sets both, on a local kind cluster. Never expose such a hub.
  • To check a refusal, use a hub with a real login and present a real token. No header overrides roles.

docs.title: After each upgrade: the roles catalog
docs.text:
Read the roles catalog for your RBAC inventory. There is no lm command for it; it needs lm_admin and lm_integrator. Mint $TOKEN as in Test the API, then:

$ curl -s https://your-hub.example.com/api/platform/roles -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    | jq -c '.roles[] | {id, wildcard}'
{"id":"lm_superadmin","wildcard":true}
{"id":"lm_admin","wildcard":false}
{"id":"lm_user","wildcard":false}

Confirm:

  • The roles listed match what the realm declares.
  • Only lm_superadmin carries wildcard: true.

One item fails: lm_integrator

lm_integrator gates the whole /api/platform/* surface plus the view and workflow applies, but it has no entry in the roles catalog. An RBAC inventory taken from the catalog misses a role that grants real access.

docs.title: Audit logging
docs.text: Every refusal leaves one WARN line naming roles and grants, never a row or a token. No refusal is written to the audit table. Refusals

docs.title: A scope-bound integrator
docs.text:
Administering a connector follows the writing rule. Every connector command (get, apply, run, pause, resume, delete, scope, and the endpoint commands) acts only on a connector whose scopes the bound integrator holds all of. lm connector list shows only those, so a connector outside those scopes, a connector spanning a scope you do not hold, or a scopeless one is simply not found. Moving a connector you hold into a scope you don't hold is refused:

$ lm connector list
NAME           TYPE         TENANT  SCHED  WINDOW  STATUS  LAST RUN
orders-ventes  hello-world  1
$ lm connector pause stock-magasin
Error: connector "stock-magasin" not found
$ lm connector scope add orders-ventes magasin
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ lm connector scope ls orders-ventes
ventes

The same hub, listed by an integrator with no scope:* role, shows stock-magasin too: unbound integrators keep administering the whole tenant.

What a connector left behind follows the same rule. A run carries counts, table names and the error message, and a dead letter carries the rejected row's values. A bound integrator's lm run list and lm dlq list show only the connectors whose scopes they hold all of. lm run get/cancel, lm dlq get/discard/replayed, and --connector/--run filters naming a connector outside those scopes answer 403.

The lm source doors create or reuse connectors, so they follow the writing rule:

  • lm csv ingest refuses a --scope you do not hold. Without --scope the one-shot lands in system, which you need to hold too.
  • Re-ingesting under the name of another scope's one-shot is refused rather than moving it into yours.
  • lm source jdbc add creates its connectors without scopes, so a bound integrator is refused before the source database is contacted. Declare the connector in a manifest with scopes: and lm apply it instead.
  • lm source jdbc list-tables lists only the connectors you hold.
  • lm source rest probe answers only for a connector you hold.
  • lm source rest from-openapi writes nothing to the hub. It drafts a manifest, and lm apply then judges its scopes:.

The capture below shows the same hub as above with two csv connectors, commandes-ventes (scopes: [ventes]) and stock-magasin (scopes: [magasin]), each run once with one malformed row. The caller is an integrator holding scope:ventes:

$ lm run list
ID        CONNECTOR         ENDPOINT  STATUS     IN  OUT  SKIPPED  DEAD-LETTERS  STARTED           ENDED
0893cee7  commandes-ventes  default   Completed  2   1    1        1             2026-10-18 15:37  2026-10-18 15:37
$ lm dlq list
ID        CONNECTOR         RUN       REASON           ATTEMPTS  RESOLUTION  MESSAGE
f8b2118f  commandes-ventes  0893cee7  MalformedSource  1                     data/commandes.csv:3 — Record has 3 values but only 2 column…
$ lm dlq get 95b20b87-d992-43e2-b08b-f50806a4d131
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ lm dlq discard 95b20b87-d992-43e2-b08b-f50806a4d131
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ lm run get b93a9839-862e-49ea-a397-f13a46751c57
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ lm csv ingest inventaire.csv --name inventaire --scope ventes
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ lm csv ingest inventaire.csv --name inventaire-bis --scope magasin
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ echo "$PGPASSWORD" | lm source jdbc add erp --url jdbc:postgresql://erp-db:5432/erp --user lumnik_reader --tables orders --password-stdin
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted

The two ids refused above are stock-magasin's dead letter and run, which an unbound integrator sees in the same lists. inventaire is a magasin one-shot. Re-ingesting it under --scope ventes would have moved it into ventes, and its rows with it.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
What lm prints Gate Fix Error: API error 403: missing role lm_integrator the platform gate, in front of every /api/platform/* path Grant lm_integrator Error: API error 403 (forbidden): no details from the server — your account may lack the required role the endpoint's role gate (an empty-body 403) Grant the role the gesture needs: the table above Error: access refused (403): scope not granted the scope gate: the caller holds scope:* roles and none matches the resource Grant the matching scope:<tag>, or remove all scope roles to go tenant-wide scope not granted on lm integration, lm notify or lm outputs outputs are tenant-wide: the caller holds any scope:* role Wire outputs as an admin with no scope:* role (Outputs) Error: connector "orders" not found, an empty lm run list or lm dlq list, or scope not granted on lm connector scope, lm run …, lm dlq … — though an unscoped account sees the connector the caller holds scope:* roles, but not every scope that connector carries Grant every scope the connector carries, or use an account with no scope role scope not granted on lm csv ingest the ingest asks for a scope the caller does not hold; without --scope it asks for system Pass --scope <tag> with a granted tag scope not granted on lm source jdbc add the guided add creates a scopeless connector Declare the connector in a manifest with scopes:, or use an account with no scope role Error: API error 404: no user record on this hub for user_id N on lm scope the token's user_id names no hub user row BYO IdP No 403 at all, even for a wrong role or no token the hub runs in dev-bypass Helm: install with auth.mode=oidc (the default) or oidc-external

An integrator bound to scope:desk, on a hub whose connectors all carry sales:

$ lm connector list
NAME  TYPE  TENANT  SCHED  WINDOW  STATUS  LAST RUN
$ lm connector get orders
Error: connector "orders" not found
$ lm csv ingest /tmp/customers.csv
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted
$ lm run get 9eb29f11-f25c-40bb-808c-4aae3c444e2c
Error: access refused (403): scope not granted

docs.title: SCIM deprovisioning
docs.text:
Your IdP pushes active: false; lumnik archives the user; the very next request is refused, even with a still-valid token. The departure half of the identity loop.

Edition

The whole /scim/v2/* surface and its token endpoints ship in lumnik Pro, the image the deploy scripts pull. They are absent from lumnik Open. Editions

sequenceDiagram
  participant I as your IdP
  participant H as hub
  participant U as user
  I->>H: PATCH /scim/v2/Users/{id} · active:false · Bearer lmscim_…
  H->>H: archive the user (archived_at)
  H-->>I: 200
  U->>H: any request, token still valid
  H-->>U: 403 {"error":"user is deactivated"}

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• JIT creates a user at first login (BYO IdP); SCIM archives the same row when your IdP deprovisions them. JIT never reactivates an archived user.
  • The integrator's departure is a different checklist: Offboarding.

docs.title: The auth model
docs.text:
• SCIM requests carry no user JWT. Each tenant mints opaque bearer tokens (lmscim_ + 32 random bytes, base64url: 256 bits); your IdP presents one on every call. The surface is not rate-limited.
  • Minting needs lm_admin, for your own tenant only. The plaintext is returned once; only its SHA-256 hash is stored, never logged, never shown again.
  • A token is scoped to one tenant and one issuer: it cannot see local users, another IdP's users, or another tenant's. Such lookups answer a SCIM 404, not a leak.
  • Missing, unknown, revoked, or a user JWT instead of a SCIM token: 401, same body in every case. The application log tells them apart: SCIM auth refused: GET /scim/v2/… reason=missing or reason=unknown-or-revoked.
$ curl -s https://<hub>/scim/v2/Users -H "Authorization: Bearer <a user JWT>"
{"schemas":["urn:ietf:params:scim:api:messages:2.0:Error"],"detail":"invalid SCIM token","status":"401"}

docs.title: Wiring your IdP
docs.text:
lm has no command for SCIM or its tokens: the gestures below are HTTP calls.

  1. Mint a token, as an lm_admin of the tenant. issuer must be the exact iss your IdP puts in its JWTs, byte for byte, or SCIM manages a parallel set of users logins never hit:

    curl -X POST "https://<hub>/api/tenants/<tid>/scim-tokens" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <your lm_admin JWT>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"issuer": "https://idp.example.com/realms/acme", "label": "okta-prod"}'
# → 201 {"id":1,"issuer":"…","label":"okta-prod","token":"lmscim_…"}   ← save the token NOW

  2. Configure the IdP's SCIM app: base URL https://<hub>/scim/v2, authentication Bearer token with the lmscim_… value, content type application/scim+json (PATCH also accepts application/json).

  3. Map attributes: externalId = the JWT subject claim (sub by default); it is the join key. userName, displayName/name and the primary emails entry are synced as profile.
  4. Verify: most IdPs test GET /scim/v2/ServiceProviderConfig, then a dedup lookup GET /scim/v2/Users?filter=userName eq "jdoe" before creating.

docs.title: The /scim/v2/Users contract
docs.text:
Verb Path Does POST /Users find-or-create by (issuer, externalId), then apply active + profile. 201. externalId required. Revives a soft-deleted user (see below); with active: true it also re-activates a user archived through the users API GET /Users/{id} one user by lumnik id. 404 if absent, deleted, or keyed to another issuer GET /Users?filter=… only externalId eq "x" and userName eq "x"; 0 or 1 result. Any other filter answers an empty list. Soft-deleted excluded, deactivated included PUT /Users/{id} full replace: active, display name, primary email PATCH /Users/{id} the deprovisioning operation: replace of top-level active only. A non-boolean active, or another op on it, is 400. Other paths are ignored DELETE /Users/{id} soft-delete, 204. The row stays, keeping the key occupied so a later login resolves to it and is refused

Deactivate vs erase

  • active: false archives. The row and its history stay; archived_at is stamped. The next request is refused, with or without a user_id claim. SCIM active: true brings the user back.
  • DELETE soft-deletes. A re-POST of the same (issuer, externalId) revives the user.
  • Neither is a GDPR erasure. The row remains until an operator removes it: GDPR & personal data.
  • A SCIM write leaves no audit row, deprovisioning included. The audit trail

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text:
• Groups: no /scim/v2/Groups. Roles are managed in the IdP realm, not pushed over SCIM.
  • Bulk, sorting, etags, changePassword: declared unsupported in ServiceProviderConfig.
  • Pagination: the only list forms are the two eq filters above.
  • The full PATCH path grammar: emails[type eq "work"].value is ignored; use PUT.
  • /Schemas and /ResourceTypes: IdPs that require schema discovery need their mappings configured by hand.
  • Unfiltered GET /Users answers an empty list, not the tenant's population.

docs.title: Token lifecycle
docs.text:
All three need lm_admin and your own tenant id in the path:

# Mint — plaintext in the response ONCE, never retrievable again
POST   /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens          {"issuer": "<idp iss>", "label": "okta-prod"}

# List active tokens — id, issuer, label, createdAt; never the hash, never the plaintext
GET    /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens

# Revoke — effective immediately, 204
DELETE /api/tenants/{tid}/scim-tokens/{id}

Rotation is mint-then-revoke: several tokens can be active at once (label tells them apart), so switching the IdP over needs no provisioning outage.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Plain 404 on every /scim/v2/* call, not the SCIM-shaped body above lumnik Open: the SCIM surface is not in that build 401 invalid SCIM token Missing Authorization: Bearer, a token never minted for this hub, a revoked one, or a user JWT. Identical response in every case 403 when minting, listing or revoking Your JWT lacks lm_admin, or the {tenantId} in the path is not your own tenant 404 on GET/PUT/PATCH/DELETE /Users/{id} No such user, soft-deleted, or the user's issuer differs from the token's: the most common wiring mistake. Compare the token's issuer with the exact iss of your IdP's JWTs (scheme, host, port, path) Dedup search finds nothing, then POST returns an existing user Normal: filters exclude soft-deleted rows, POST is find-or-create Deactivated user can still call the API A request already executing finishes; every request after it is denied. If later calls still succeed, confirm the PATCH landed (GET /Users/{id} → "active": false) and the issuer matches
